Each telescope and wavelength of light offers unique information. Hubble’s visible-light view shows the cat-shaped dust filament as dark brown and opaque against a colorful gas backdrop. An ionization front on the right side of the “cat” highlights where dust is being heated and essentially evaporated. Webb’s infrared-light reveals faint background dust pillars that are unseen in visible light. In mid-infrared light, the emission from the warm dust, which is being excited by starlight, shines brightly. Moving to the near-infrared view, Webb pierces through some of the dust to reveal many stars. In each image, the cat’s eye, which is most likely a young star embedded in the dust, glows brightly. The Cat’s Head Nebula is a temporary scene that will eventually disperse, but in the meantime, Hubble and Webb’s views of the nebula are helping scientists learn more about the complexities of star formation.

meta.description: This tour simultaneously glides through imagery from NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes of the Cat’s Head Nebula. The dust filament broadly remains the same in shape across the different wavelengths of light, but each view contains different details. Hubble’s visible-light image shows the “cat” as an opaque, dark brown pillar with a glowing red eye—most likely a young star embedded in the dust. Webb’s infrared observations reveal some of the cat’s structure and faint background filaments of dust to its left. In near-infrared light, Webb pierces through some of the dust to reveal many stars and even background galaxies. In mid-infrared light, the telescope images the emission from warm dust and carbon-based molecules excited by starlight.

meta.description:
In 2024, global temperatures for June through August were the hottest on record, narrowly topping the same period in 2023. The exceptional heat extended throughout other seasons, too, with global temperatures breaking records for 15 straight months from June 2023 until August 2024, according to scientists from NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS).
Although this spell of record heat fits within a long-term warming trend driven by human activity—primarily greenhouse gas emissions—the intensity of the heat, which reached a crescendo in the last half of 2023, surprised leading climate scientists. In a commentary in Nature, Gavin Schmidt, the director of GISS, used words like “humbling” and “confounding” to explain just how far temperatures overshot expectations during that period.
The charts on this page show how much global temperatures in 2023 and 2024 diverged from expectations based on NASA’s temperature record. Roughly a year later, Schmidt and other climatologists are still trying to understand why.

The gather began Oct. 2 and finished yesterday with eight horses gathered. 
The Warm Springs Herd Management Area comprises about 475,000 acres of public land south of Hines, Oregon. That range area can sustain 96 to 178 horses.

meta.credit: Kiger wild horse auction, Hines, Oregon
meta.description:
The Kiger herd auction report: 151 wild horses adopted; highest winning bid was $10,500; and bidders came to the auction in Hines, Oregon, from as far away as New Zealand!
Horses not adopted at the Oct. 3 event will be made available for online adoption here: www.blm.gov/adoptahorse 
Wild horses from the Kiger and Riddle Mountain herd management areas in southeastern Oregon were gathered in late August, 2015.
The Kiger horses, as they are commonly known, have had an almost 100 percent adoption rate since 1986. The respective Appropriate Management Level (AML) herd sizes are 33 head for the Riddle HMA and 51 for the Kiger HMA. Due to the small herd size, popularity and adoptability, PZP contraceptives and returning/releasing geldings into the wild are not considered for these herds. The goal of this gather is for the range to achieve or maintain a thriving ecological balance.
More information on the wild horse program in the BLM Burns District: www.blm.gov/or/districts/burns/wildhorse/

Photos and video: BLM Volunteer Cathleen Shea
